nameStory: The cinnamon rose gets its name from the reddish-brown bark on its stems, which resembles the color of ground cinnamon spice. This warm, russet hue is especially noticeable on young shoots and makes the shrub distinctive even when not in bloom.
description: Cinnamon rose is a deciduous shrub that typically grows up to 6 feet tall, forming dense thickets through underground runners. Originally from northern Europe and Siberia, this hardy rose has naturalized in some parts of New England after escaping from old gardens. It produces simple pink flowers in late spring, followed by round, red hips that persist into winter and are rich in vitamin C.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Young stems have distinctive cinnamon-colored bark that peels slightly, giving them a warm reddish-brown appearance that's especially striking in winter sunlight.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Simple pink flowers with 5 petals bloom in late spring, about 2 inches across, with a sweet fragrance and prominent yellow centers full of stamens.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Round red hips about the size of small cherries ripen in late summer and persist through winter, feeling firm and smooth to the touch.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves have 5-7 oval leaflets with finely toothed edges that feel slightly rough and have a matte finish rather than glossy.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense colonies through underground runners, creating thickets of upright stems armed with straight, sharp thorns.

habitat: Look for cinnamon rose in old garden sites, abandoned farmsteads, and naturalized areas where it has escaped cultivation. It prefers moist, well-drained soils and can tolerate partial shade, often found along woodland edges or in clearings.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge in late April, followed by fragrant pink blooms in late May to early June that attract bees and other pollinators.
seasonality.summer: Flowers fade and green hips begin forming, while the foliage remains full and green throughout the hot months.
seasonality.fall: Hips ripen to bright red and leaves may turn yellow before dropping, leaving the colorful fruit visible on bare stems.
seasonality.winter: The cinnamon-colored bark is most noticeable, and persistent red hips provide winter interest and food for birds.

funFact: The vitamin C-rich hips of cinnamon rose were so valued during World War II that British schoolchildren were organized to collect them by the ton to make rose hip syrup, helping prevent scurvy when citrus fruits were scarce.
confusionNotes: Distinguished from other wild roses by its distinctive cinnamon-colored bark and tendency to form dense colonies. Most other roses have green or grayish bark, and few spread as aggressively through underground runners.
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name Rosa majalis is often confused with Rosa cinnamomea in older plant guides, and both names have been applied to different rose species over time. What's called 'cinnamon rose' in New England gardens may actually be this species or a close relative.
compareHints: Unlike the common multiflora rose with its clusters of small white flowers, cinnamon rose has larger, solitary pink blooms. It's less thorny than rugosa rose and spreads more aggressively than most native roses like Carolina rose or Virginia rose. The cinnamon-colored bark is unique among New England roses.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England roses, multiflora rose is unique for its enormous flower clusters (other roses have flowers in smaller groups or singly) and those telltale fringed stipules.
Rugosa rose stands apart from other New England roses with its unmistakable wrinkled leaves - no other rose species has this corrugated texture.

Among New England's wild roses, swamp rose is unique in its preference for wet habitats - while Carolina rose and Virginia rose stick to drier areas, and multiflora rose (an invasive) has much denser thorns and forms larger, more aggressive colonies.
Among New England's wild roses, Carolina rose is the champion spreader, forming low colonies while relatives like swamp rose grow taller and more upright.
Among New England's wild roses, Virginian rose stands out for its glossy leaflets (rugosa rose has wrinkled leaves) and typically 7-9 leaflets per leaf (most others have fewer).

Among New England's roses, Sherard's downy-rose stands out for its compact size and distinctly grayish, downy leaves - most other wild roses like swamp rose or Carolina rose have greener, smoother foliage.

Among New England's wild roses, smooth rose is unique for its nearly thornless stems – multiflora rose has curved thorns, rugosa rose has dense straight prickles, and swamp rose has scattered thorns along its stems.
Among New England's roses, dog-rose stands out for its large, curved thorns and smooth leaflets without fuzzy coating.
Memorial rose is unique among New England roses for its prostrate, ground-hugging growth habit - all other rose species in the region grow as upright shrubs.
Among New England's wild roses, shining rose is uniquely low-growing and has by far the glossiest leaves.
Among New England's wild roses, prickly wild rose stands out for its extreme thorniness — it has far more prickles per inch than rugosa rose, swamp rose, or any of our other native roses.
Among New England's roses, sweet-brier is the only one with apple-scented leaves - this fragrance alone separates it from multiflora rose, rugosa rose, and native species.
Climbing prairie rose stands out from other New England roses primarily by its vigorous climbing habit with long, flexible canes.
Unlike New England's native roses such as swamp rose or Carolina rose which have green leaves, red-leaved rose's blue-gray to purplish foliage is unmistakable.
